They scaled their infrastructure in 2 patterns -

They switched from pattern 1 to 2 for scalability, decoupling, and security. [q-74] [q-116] [q-117]

Their cloud service receives task requests, sends them to an SQS (Amazon's Queue Service) queue, and returns an HTTP 202 response. 
 A Lambda worker (serverless process runner) then processes each queued task and runs the agent until completion. [q-72]

[q-21] The selected issues fall into four recurring categories. (1) Sandbox and security-boundary regressions across OS backends: the Linux migration to bubblewrap, Windows sandbox helpers, and read-scope expectations. (2) Unbounded resource growth and leaks: SQLite log writes, orphaned MCP processes, and session-history scans. (3) Client/backend transport and schema contract mismatches: Responses API 404s, WebSocket policy closes, remote-compaction failures, enum/schema drift, and shared app-server state polluting other surfaces. (4) Release and packaging regressions from a very fast release cadence: missing npm optional packages, MUSL arm64 segfaults, and the Windows daemon privilege error. Together they point to a weak spot: one shared harness ships to many surfaces and platforms faster than cross-platform tests can cover. Maintainers usually respond with quick alpha or point-release fixes, and sometimes with architectural changes such as moving compaction to the client.
